nameStory: This tiny freshwater alga doesn't have a widely-used common name, so we'll call it creeping threadwort - a name that captures its creeping growth habit and thread-like appearance. The scientific name Aphanochaete comes from Greek words meaning 'invisible bristles,' referring to the microscopic hair-like structures that are hard to see without magnification.
description: Creeping threadwort is a microscopic freshwater green alga that forms thin, creeping mats on submerged surfaces. You'll need a hand lens or microscope to really see its structure, which consists of branching threads of cells that spread along rocks, wood, or other underwater surfaces. Individual threads are incredibly thin - much finer than human hair - and typically form patches just a few millimeters across.

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms thin, creeping mats that spread horizontally along submerged surfaces, feeling slightly slimy to the touch

idTips.label: Thread structure
idTips.description: Individual filaments are extremely fine and branching, visible only with magnification, creating a delicate web-like pattern

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to yellowish-green when healthy, may appear brownish when stressed or dying

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels slightly slippery and smooth when touched underwater, not rough or fuzzy like some other algae

habitat: Found in clean, cool freshwater streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England, typically attached to rocks, submerged logs, or other hard surfaces in shallow water. Prefers areas with good water circulation and moderate light levels, often in the same spots where you might find watercress or other aquatic plants.

seasonality.spring: Begins active growth as water temperatures rise, forming small patches on submerged surfaces. Most easily spotted when water levels are lower and surfaces are more exposed.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when mats are most extensive and vibrant green. Best time for observation as the alga is most active and visible.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows and patches may become less vibrant as temperatures drop. Still present but may be harder to distinguish from other algae.
seasonality.winter: Survives under ice in a dormant state, virtually invisible until spring growth resumes. Look for small remnant patches in warmer microhabitats.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, this little alga is actually a master architect - it can sense the direction of water flow and deliberately grows its branches upstream to capture more nutrients, essentially 'farming' the current like an underwater spider spinning its web!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other thread-like freshwater algae like Stigeoclonium, but creeping threadwort grows in flat, creeping mats rather than upright tufts. Remember: if it's hugging the surface like a green carpet rather than waving in the current like hair, you're probably looking at creeping threadwort.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of observations in New England (only one recorded!) suggests this species may be easily overlooked rather than truly rare, as most people don't examine microscopic algae closely. It could also indicate this species prefers very specific water conditions that are uncommon in our region.
compareHints: As the only Aphanochaete species documented in New England, compare it with other creeping freshwater algae in the order Chaetophorales. Unlike the more common Stigeoclonium which forms upright, branching tufts, creeping threadwort stays flat against surfaces. It's also much more delicate and less visible than the robust mats formed by Cladophora species.
